prompt: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium?

options.text: Pulmonary veins
Pulmonary arteries
Superior vena cava
Coronary sinus

explanation: Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulmonary arteries go to the lungs with deoxygenated blood.
distractorExplanations.c: SVC returns systemic venous blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Coronary sinus drains heart venous blood.

prompt: The outermost layer of a vein/artery wall is the

options.text: Tunica intima (endothelium)
Tunica externa (adventitia)
Tunica media (smooth muscle)
Epicardium (visceral layer)

explanation: Vessels have intima, media, and externa; myocardium/endocardium are heart layers.

distractorExplanations.a: The tunica intima is the innermost endothelial lining in contact with blood, not the outermost layer of the vessel wall.
distractorExplanations.c: The tunica media is the middle smooth-muscle layer that changes vessel diameter; the externa (adventitia) lies outside it.
distractorExplanations.d: The epicardium is the outer layer of the heart wall, not of veins and arteries, whose outer layer is the tunica externa.

Plasma albumin

Lymphocytes

prompt: Serum differs from plasma in that serum

options.text: Contains fibrinogen because no anticoagulant is added
Is collected in EDTA tubes and spun right away
Contains the anticoagulant used during collection
Lacks clotting factors consumed when blood clots

explanation: Plasma is from anticoagulated blood; serum is from clotted blood after factors are consumed. No anticoagulant is used when collecting serum.

distractorExplanations.a: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and consumed in the clot, so serum lacks it; plasma from anticoagulated blood retains fibrinogen.
distractorExplanations.b: EDTA is an anticoagulant, so an EDTA tube yields whole blood or plasma; serum requires a clotted specimen in a tube without anticoagulant.
distractorExplanations.c: Plasma contains the tube's anticoagulant; serum comes from blood allowed to clot with no anticoagulant added.

options.text: Median cubital, cephalic, and basilic veins
Cephalic, basilic, and great saphenous veins
Brachial artery, median nerve, and basilic vein
Dorsal metacarpal veins on the back of the hand

explanation: Standard AC veins are median cubital, cephalic, and basilic; arteries are avoided for routine venipuncture.

distractorExplanations.b: The great saphenous vein runs in the leg, not the antecubital fossa; the third AC vein used for venipuncture is the median cubital.
distractorExplanations.c: The brachial artery and median nerve lie in the AC fossa as structures to avoid; they are never targets for routine venipuncture.
distractorExplanations.d: Dorsal hand veins are an alternate site when AC veins are unsuitable; they are outside the antecubital fossa.

prompt: Hemostasis refers to:

options.text: The breakdown of a clot after healing
The process that stops bleeding
The rupture of red cells in a specimen
The formation of blood cells in marrow

explanation: Hemostasis includes vascular spasm, platelet plug, and coagulation.

distractorExplanations.a: Breaking down a clot after the vessel heals is fibrinolysis, the step that follows hemostasis rather than hemostasis itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Rupture of red blood cells is hemolysis, a specimen-quality problem, not the body's process of stopping bleeding.
distractorExplanations.d: Formation of blood cells in the bone marrow is hematopoiesis; hemostasis is vascular spasm, platelet plug, and coagulation.

Left ventricle
Left atrium

prompt: Capillaries are specialized for:

options.text: Storing elastic energy to maintain arterial pressure
Returning blood to the heart through one-way valves
Regulating blood flow by constricting their muscular walls
Exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes with tissues

explanation: Thin capillary walls enable exchange; arteries are conduit/pressure vessels.

distractorExplanations.b: Returning blood through one-way valves describes veins; capillaries are single-cell-thick vessels without valves.
distractorExplanations.c: Capillaries lack smooth muscle; arterioles and precapillary sphincters regulate flow into capillary beds.

Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport
Platelet plug formation at injury
Maintaining plasma oncotic pressure

explanation: WBCs defend against pathogens; oxygen is RBC/hemoglobin role.

distractorExplanations.b: Gas transport is the job of erythrocytes (red cells) and their hemoglobin, not leukocytes, which defend against infection.
distractorExplanations.c: Forming a platelet plug is the role of thrombocytes (platelets) in hemostasis, not of white blood cells.
distractorExplanations.d: Plasma oncotic pressure is maintained mainly by albumin, a plasma protein, not by leukocytes.

prompt: Why are veins preferred over arteries for routine blood collection?

options.text: Venous blood has higher oxygen content, which most tests require
Thinner walls, lower pressure, and more accessible superficial locations
Veins have thicker muscular walls that seal quickly after the needle is removed
Arteries lie superficially but carry a higher risk of hemolysis

explanation: Venipuncture targets veins for safety and accessibility; arterial puncture is specialized.

distractorExplanations.a: Systemic venous blood is deoxygenated; veins are chosen for safety and access, and reference ranges are set for venous samples.
distractorExplanations.c: Arteries, not veins, have the thick muscular walls; veins are preferred because their walls are thinner and pressure is low.
distractorExplanations.d: Arteries generally lie deeper than veins; the arterial risk is high pressure, bleeding, and nerve injury, not hemolysis.

options.text: Inferior vena cava

Superior vena cava
Brachiocephalic artery

prompt: Which statement about capillaries is correct?

options.text: They are microscopic vessels where exchange of gases/nutrients occurs
They carry blood away from the heart under the highest pressure
They contain one-way valves that prevent backflow in the limbs
They yield skin-puncture blood that matches venous blood exactly

explanation: Capillary beds enable exchange; skin punctures collect capillary blood (with interstitial/arterial mix). Skin punctures collect capillary blood mixed with tissue fluid.

distractorExplanations.b: Carrying blood away from the heart at the highest pressure describes arteries; capillary pressure is far lower.
distractorExplanations.c: One-way valves are a feature of medium and large veins in the limbs; capillaries have no valves.
distractorExplanations.d: Dermal puncture blood is a mix of arterial, venous, and tissue fluid, closer to arterial; values such as glucose differ from venous.

prompt: Blood pressure is highest in which vessel type under normal physiology?

options.text: Veins (especially the venae cavae)
Arteries (especially aorta/large arteries)
Capillaries (especially in the skin)
Arterioles (especially in the kidney cortex)

explanation: Arterial pressure is highest; veins are low-pressure capacitance vessels.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure is lowest in the large veins near the right atrium; veins are low-pressure capacitance vessels.
distractorExplanations.c: Capillary pressure is much lower than arterial pressure because most of the drop occurs across the arterioles upstream.
distractorExplanations.d: Arterioles are where pressure falls most steeply, so their pressure is lower than in the aorta and large arteries.

options.text: The radial artery and radial nerve
The cephalic vein and lateral cutaneous nerve
The brachial artery and median nerve
The axillary artery and brachial plexus

explanation: Medial AC anatomy places basilic near artery/nerve—use caution or choose safer veins first.

Sodium fluoride

prompt: The correct CLSI order of draw begins with:

options.text: Light-blue citrate tube, since coagulation tests come first
Blood culture bottles/SPS when cultures are ordered
Red or gold serum tube to clear air from the tubing
Lavender EDTA tube, since CBCs are the most ordered test

Gauge = needle length, not diameter

Higher gauge = smaller diameter lumen

options.text: To maintain the required 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio
To dilute coagulation factors intentionally
Because underfilling speeds clotting usefully
Citrate volume is decorative

prompt: A gray-top tube with sodium fluoride is commonly used for:

options.text: Potassium testing on delayed specimens to prevent leakage
Glucose testing when glycolysis inhibition is needed
Coagulation testing when platelet activation must be blocked
Ammonia testing when the sample cannot be put on ice

explanation: Fluoride inhibits glycolysis preserving glucose; oxalate/EDTA variants exist by manufacturer.

prompt: Tourniquet application should generally not exceed

options.text: About 30 seconds before the draw
About 45 seconds before the draw
About one minute before the draw
About three minutes before the draw

explanation: Prolonged tourniquet time causes hemoconcentration and analyte changes.

distractorExplanations.a: The CLSI limit is one minute; 30 seconds is a common misbelief, and the tourniquet may stay on up to a minute while the vein is located.
distractorExplanations.b: The accepted maximum is one minute, not 45 seconds; beyond one minute hemoconcentration begins to alter results.
distractorExplanations.d: Three minutes far exceeds the one-minute limit and causes hemoconcentration that falsely raises proteins and protein-bound analytes.

prompt: Which action reduces needle needlestick risk after a draw?

options.text: Recapping with the one-handed scoop method before disposal
Removing the needle from the holder to reuse the holder
Activating the safety feature once the tubes are labeled
Activating the engineered safety feature immediately

explanation: OSHA-aligned practice forbids two-handed recapping and improper disposal. The whole assembly then goes straight into a sharps container.

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA allows recapping only when no alternative exists; after venipuncture the safety feature is activated instead of recapping.
distractorExplanations.b: OSHA requires the tube holder to be discarded with the needle attached; unscrewing the needle for holder reuse causes sticks.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying activation until after labeling leaves a contaminated needle exposed; it must be activated immediately after withdrawal.

prompt: Serum separator tubes (SST) contain

options.text: Clot activator and gel separator
EDTA and gel separator
Lithium heparin and gel separator
Clot activator without a gel barrier

explanation: SST allows clotting then gel barrier separation of serum after centrifugation.

distractorExplanations.b: EDTA with gel is the plasma preparation tube (PPT, pearl/white top) used for molecular tests, not the serum separator tube.
distractorExplanations.c: Lithium heparin with gel is the plasma separator tube (PST, light green); the SST has clot activator for serum.
distractorExplanations.d: Clot activator without gel describes the plastic red-top serum tube; the SST adds a gel barrier that separates serum after spinning.

options.text: Use a transfer device and push the plunger to speed filling
Use a transfer device and allow vacuum to fill tubes without forcing
Puncture stoppers with the syringe needle and let vacuum draw it in
Use a transfer device and fill tubes in any order since draw is done

explanation: Forcing causes hemolysis; transfer devices improve safety.

distractorExplanations.c: Using the syringe needle to pierce stoppers risks needlesticks; OSHA-aligned practice requires a safety transfer device.

options.text: Drawing large volumes quickly for blood donor units
Drawing from large, easy antecubital veins in healthy adults
Drawing from small/fragile veins or hand veins with better control
Drawing citrate tubes first, since no discard tube is needed

explanation: Butterflies aid difficult veins; ID and order of draw still apply; ABGs need specialized training.

18-gauge (smaller gauge number = larger diameter)

options.text: Contain clot activator and gel for serum chemistry
Contain lithium heparin and gel for plasma chemistry
Contain clot activator only, for blood bank testing
Contain sodium citrate and gel for coagulation tests

prompt: A gray-top tube with sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate is commonly used for:

options.text: CBC testing when cell morphology must be preserved
Glucose testing when glycolysis inhibition is needed
PT/INR testing when calcium must be bound by citrate
Lipid testing when the patient could not fast

explanation: Fluoride inhibits glycolysis; gray tops are classic glucose/alcohol (policy) tubes—not CBC/coag/cultures.

prompt: When using a syringe draw transferred to evacuated tubes, the phlebotomist should?

options.text: Puncture the stoppers with the syringe needle while holding the tube in your hand
Remove the stoppers and pour blood in slowly to avoid hemolysis
Transfer using a transfer device—never force blood into tubes
Use a transfer device and fill tubes in reverse order of draw

explanation: Safety transfer devices prevent needlesticks; order of draw still applies when filling tubes.

options.text: At the bedside immediately after collection with two identifiers per policy
At the bedside just before collection so tubes are ready to fill
At the nursing station after collection, using the requisition labels
In the lab on receipt, matching tubes to the requisition by order time

explanation: Bedside labeling prevents wrong-patient errors.

prompt: A specimen for cold agglutinin testing may require

options.text: Chilling in an ice slurry and delivery within 15 minutes
Warming/transport at body temperature per lab instructions
Protection from light with foil or an amber tube
Holding at room temperature for 30 minutes before spinning

explanation: Some analytes require temperature control (warm, chilled, protected from light)

distractorExplanations.a: Ice slurry is for ammonia and lactate; chilling makes cold agglutinins bind red cells and gives falsely low results.
distractorExplanations.c: Light protection is needed for bilirubin and similar photosensitive analytes, not for cold agglutinin specimens.
distractorExplanations.d: Room temperature lets cold agglutinins start binding red cells; the specimen must be kept at 37 °C until the serum is separated.

prompt: Photosensitive analytes (e.g., bilirubin) should be

options.text: Chilled in an ice slurry during transport
Kept at 37 °C during transport
Protected from light during transport
Spun within 15 minutes of collection

explanation: Light degrades certain analytes; amber tubes or wrapping are used.

distractorExplanations.a: Ice slurry transport is for ammonia, lactate, and similar unstable analytes; bilirubin's problem is degradation by light.
distractorExplanations.b: Body-temperature transport is for cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins; bilirubin needs protection from light.
distractorExplanations.d: Rapid separation does not protect bilirubin from light; the tube must be wrapped in foil or collected in an amber tube.

prompt: Hemoconcentration from prolonged tourniquet can falsely elevate

options.text: Glucose and other small, freely diffusing molecules
Sodium and chloride from plasma water loss
Urea from reduced kidney filtration
Proteins and protein-bound substances

explanation: Plasma water leaves the vein, concentrating cells/proteins. It can also contribute to potassium changes.

distractorExplanations.a: Small, freely diffusing analytes move out with plasma water, so they change little; large proteins and bound substances concentrate.
distractorExplanations.b: Electrolytes like sodium and chloride diffuse freely with water, so hemoconcentration changes them minimally.
distractorExplanations.c: A tourniquet does not change kidney filtration; urea is small and freely diffusible, so stasis barely affects it.

prompt: If a specimen is lipemic, it means:

options.text: Cloudy/milky serum/plasma often from recent fat intake or metabolic causes
Red or pink serum/plasma from red cells ruptured during the collection process
Dark yellow or brown serum/plasma from high bilirubin levels
Serum/plasma that contains small fibrin clots after spinning

explanation: Lipemia can interfere with optical assays; fasting may be required.

distractorExplanations.b: Red or pink serum indicates hemolysis from ruptured red cells; lipemia is milky turbidity caused by lipids.
distractorExplanations.c: Dark yellow or brown serum is icteric, caused by high bilirubin; lipemic serum is cloudy or milky from fats.
distractorExplanations.d: Fibrin strands come from incomplete clotting before centrifugation; lipemia refers to milky turbidity from lipids.

prompt: Chain of custody is most critical for:

options.text: STAT specimens where turnaround time must be documented
Forensic/toxicology specimens where legal integrity must be documented
Blood bank specimens where the patient armband must match
Send-out reference lab specimens where courier pickup times must be logged

explanation: COC documents handling for legal acceptability of results.

distractorExplanations.a: STAT tracking documents speed of testing, not the legal handling record; chain of custody is for forensic and drug-testing specimens.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood bank identification bands ensure transfusion safety, but they are not a legal chain-of-custody record.
distractorExplanations.d: Courier logs track shipping; chain of custody is the signed, unbroken handling record required for legally defensible results.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Centrifugation of a serum tube should occur

options.text: Immediately after collection to prevent glycolysis in the tube
Within 5 minutes, since clot activator works instantly
After the specimen has fully clotted per tube instructions
After 4 hours at room temperature so the clot can retract

explanation: Premature spin of serum tubes can trap fibrin and harm quality.

distractorExplanations.a: Serum tubes must clot first (about 30–60 minutes); spinning immediately leaves fibrin in the serum and degrades specimen quality.
distractorExplanations.b: Clot activator shortens clotting to about 30 minutes; it does not work instantly, so a 5-minute spin is premature.
distractorExplanations.d: Serum should be separated from cells within 2 hours; a 4-hour delay lets glucose fall and potassium leak from cells.

prompt: A rejected specimen due to hemolysis should lead the phlebotomist to:

options.text: Recollect using a smaller 25-gauge needle to slow the blood flow
Recollect and shake the tubes well to mix the additive
Ask the lab to run it with a hemolysis comment
Recollect properly after reviewing technique causes

explanation: Hemolysis invalidates many tests; recollect and improve technique.

distractorExplanations.a: Very small needles increase hemolysis by shearing red cells; a 21–23G needle is appropriate for most adult recollections.
distractorExplanations.b: Vigorous shaking ruptures red cells; additive tubes are mixed by gentle inversion, which is one of the technique fixes.
distractorExplanations.c: A rejected hemolyzed specimen is not run with a comment; hemolysis falsely raises potassium and other analytes, so recollect.

prompt: Ammonia and lactic acid specimens often require

options.text: Chilling and prompt processing per laboratory protocol
Warming to body temperature until the lab receives them
Wrapping in foil to protect the specimen from light
Letting the tube clot 30 minutes at room temperature first

explanation: These analytes are unstable; ice slurry and rapid analysis are common requirements.

distractorExplanations.b: Warming to 37 °C is for cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins; ammonia and lactate rise unless chilled and processed quickly.
distractorExplanations.c: Foil wrapping protects light-sensitive analytes such as bilirubin; ammonia and lactate need chilling and fast processing.
distractorExplanations.d: A 30-minute room-temperature wait lets ammonia and lactate rise from cell metabolism; these are plasma tests sent on ice.

prompt: Aliquoting a specimen means:

options.text: Pouring blood from one additive tube into another to top it up
Dividing plasma/serum into secondary tubes for testing/storage
Spinning the specimen to separate cells from serum or plasma
Labeling the primary tube with the accession number in the lab

explanation: Aliquots allow multiple tests while preserving primary tube integrity rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Pouring between additive tubes contaminates additives and changes ratios; aliquoting divides separated serum or plasma.
distractorExplanations.c: Spinning to separate cells is centrifugation, the step before aliquoting, not aliquoting itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigning and labeling an accession number is accessioning; aliquoting splits serum or plasma into secondary tubes.

prompt: Cold agglutinins specimens often require

options.text: Placing the specimen in an ice slurry right away to stabilize the antibodies
Holding the specimen at room temperature, like most routine chemistry tubes
Keeping the specimen warm (body temperature) as directed until processing
Wrapping the specimen in foil to shield it from light until processing

explanation: Cold agglutinins can precipitate in the cold—follow warm-handling instructions.

distractorExplanations.a: Ice slurry is for ammonia and lactate; chilling makes cold agglutinins attach to red cells and lowers the measured titer.
distractorExplanations.b: Room temperature is cool enough for cold agglutinins to bind red cells; the specimen must stay at body temperature.
distractorExplanations.d: Foil protects photosensitive analytes such as bilirubin; cold agglutinin specimens need warmth, not light protection.

prompt: Which analyte is commonly elevated by prolonged fist clenching/pumping during venipuncture?

options.text: Sodium, from sweat produced while pumping
Glucose, from muscle release of stored sugar
Bilirubin, from red cells crushed by the fist
Potassium (and other muscle-related changes)

explanation: Muscle activity can raise potassium and affect other results—avoid pumping.

distractorExplanations.a: Fist pumping does not raise serum sodium; muscle contraction releases potassium from muscle cells into the blood.
distractorExplanations.b: Working muscle consumes glucose rather than releasing it into the vein; the classic pumping artifact is a falsely high potassium.
distractorExplanations.c: Clenching does not crush red cells into bilirubin; bilirubin is unaffected, while potassium rises from muscle activity.

prompt: Bilirubin specimens are often protected from light because light can

options.text: Degrade bilirubin and falsely lower results
Oxidize bilirubin and falsely raise results
Hemolyze red cells and falsely raise results
Activate platelets and form clots in serum

explanation: Light-sensitive analytes need amber tubes/wraps as specified.

distractorExplanations.b: Light breaks down bilirubin, so results fall rather than rise; the error direction is falsely low, not high.
distractorExplanations.c: Light exposure does not rupture red cells; the concern is photodegradation of bilirubin, which lowers results.
distractorExplanations.d: Light does not activate platelets or cause clotting; bilirubin specimens are shielded because light degrades bilirubin.

prompt: A specimen rejected for improper labeling should be

options.text: Relabeled by the collector after confirming the patient's name
Recollected with correct bedside labeling per policy
Tested and reported with a comment noting the label error
Held until the nurse verifies which patient it came from

explanation: Mislabeled specimens are patient-safety events; recollect rather than guess. Never relabel a tube after it leaves the bedside.

distractorExplanations.a: Once a tube leaves the bedside, its identity cannot be confirmed; relabeling a mislabeled specimen risks a wrong-patient result.
distractorExplanations.c: A comment does not make a mislabeled result safe; rejected specimens are recollected, not reported with a disclaimer.
distractorExplanations.d: After-the-fact verification cannot prove which patient a tube came from; policy requires recollection with bedside labeling.

prompt: Which statement about blood culture collection is correct?

options.text: Cleanse the site with alcohol and fill the anaerobic bottle first when using a butterfly
Draw the cultures after the antibiotic dose so the bottles capture peak levels
Cleanse the site thoroughly with appropriate antiseptic and fill bottles to correct volumes
Cleanse the site, then repalpate with a gloved finger to confirm the vein before puncture

explanation: Aseptic prep and correct volume maximize pathogen recovery and minimize contamination. Do not touch the sterile bottle tops with nonsterile items.

distractorExplanations.a: With a butterfly, the aerobic bottle is filled first because tubing air would enter the anaerobic bottle; the order here is reversed.
distractorExplanations.b: Blood cultures are drawn before antibiotics start; antibiotics in the sample suppress growth and cause false-negative cultures.
distractorExplanations.d: Repalpating after antiseptic prep recontaminates the site unless a sterile glove is used or the site is prepped again.

prompt: The most important step before venipuncture is

options.text: Identify the patient with two identifiers and verify the order
Identify the patient by name and room number from the requisition
Confirm the patient's fasting status before checking the wristband
Ask 'Are you Mr. Smith?' and proceed if the patient says yes

explanation: Wrong-patient draws are critical errors; follow facility ID policy including unconscious patients.

distractorExplanations.b: A room number is not an acceptable identifier because patients move; two identifiers such as full name and DOB are required.
distractorExplanations.c: Fasting status matters for some tests, but identity is confirmed first; a perfect specimen from the wrong patient is a critical error.
distractorExplanations.d: A leading yes/no question lets confused patients agree; the patient should state their full name and DOB to match the requisition.

prompt: A patient feels faint during a draw. The phlebotomist should

options.text: Finish filling the current tube, then lower the head between the knees
Stop the draw, protect from fall, and place them supine if needed
Stop the draw and have them walk to the waiting area for fresh air
Stop the draw and offer ammonia inhalants to revive the patient

explanation: Vasovagal syncope needs immediate safety measures and discontinuation as needed.

distractorExplanations.a: The draw must stop at once; finishing the tube risks injury, and head-between-knees positioning can lead to a fall.
distractorExplanations.c: Walking a faint patient risks a fall; they should stay seated or lie supine under observation until recovered.
distractorExplanations.d: CLSI advises against ammonia inhalants because they can trigger respiratory problems; positioning and observation come first.

prompt: Standard Precautions during phlebotomy include

options.text: Gloves only when the patient has a known bloodborne infection
Gloves for draws, changed between patients when visibly soiled
Gloves for draws and hand hygiene before/after glove use
Gown, mask, and gloves for every routine venipuncture

explanation: All blood is potentially infectious; gloves are single-use.

distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions treat all blood as potentially infectious; gloves are worn for every draw, not only for known infections.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are single-use and changed between every patient, soiled or not, with hand hygiene after removal.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine venipuncture requires gloves and hand hygiene; gowns and masks are added for splash risk or transmission-based precautions.

prompt: If a patient refuses a blood draw, the correct action is

options.text: Explain the doctor's order again and draw once the patient stops objecting
Draw anyway since the provider's order implies the patient's consent
Leave the requisition at the bedside and try again on the next round
Do not force the procedure; document and notify the appropriate clinician/staff

explanation: Competent refusal must be respected; coercion and wrong-patient draws are unethical/illegal.

distractorExplanations.a: A patient who stops objecting has not consented; a competent refusal is respected, documented, and reported to the clinician.
distractorExplanations.b: A provider's order does not override a competent patient's refusal; drawing anyway can constitute assault and battery.
distractorExplanations.c: Quietly retrying later skips the required steps; the refusal must be documented and the nurse or provider notified.

prompt: Mastectomy on the left side means venipuncture should generally

options.text: Avoid the left arm (same side) unless a physician specifically approves
Use the left arm if the mastectomy was more than five years ago
Use the left hand veins, since only the antecubital area is affected
Use the left arm with a lighter tourniquet to protect the lymph nodes

explanation: Same-side draws risk lymphedema/infection concerns; choose alternate site per policy.

distractorExplanations.b: Lymphedema risk from node removal is lifelong; time since surgery does not lift the same-side restriction without approval.
distractorExplanations.c: The whole same-side arm, including hand veins, is affected by impaired lymphatic drainage, not just the antecubital area.
distractorExplanations.d: A lighter tourniquet does not remove the lymphedema and infection risk; the same-side arm is avoided unless a physician approves.

prompt: Iatrogenic anemia is a risk when:

options.text: Tubes are underfilled, causing improper additive ratios
Excessive cumulative blood volumes are drawn
Tourniquets stay on longer than one minute
Small-gauge needles hemolyze red cells in the vein

explanation: Frequent large draws can cause anemia; pediatric volumes are carefully limited. Infants and critically ill patients are most at risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Underfilled tubes distort additive ratios and test results but reduce, not increase, the blood removed from the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Prolonged tourniquet time causes hemoconcentration in the specimen; it does not remove blood volume from the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemolysis from small needles occurs in the specimen, not the circulation, and is a quality problem rather than a cause of anemia.

prompt: Which is appropriate patient communication before a draw?

options.text: Tell the patient it won't hurt at all so they stay relaxed
Explain what each test will diagnose so the patient understands
Explain the procedure briefly and obtain consent/cooperation
Skip the explanation if the order is signed, to save the patient time

explanation: Brief honest explanation builds trust; do not guarantee zero pain or over-interpret tests.

distractorExplanations.a: Promising no pain is dishonest and erodes trust when the stick hurts; explain briefly that there may be a quick pinch.
distractorExplanations.b: Interpreting tests and their diagnostic meaning is the provider's role; the phlebotomist explains the procedure itself.
distractorExplanations.d: A signed order does not replace the patient's informed cooperation; a brief explanation is still needed before every draw.

prompt: A hematoma forming during venipuncture should prompt

options.text: Redirect the needle deeper to find the vein, then apply pressure
Loosen the tourniquet and keep drawing to finish the tubes
Remove the needle first, then release tourniquet and apply pressure
Release tourniquet, remove needle, and apply pressure

explanation: Expanding hematoma means stop and hold pressure to limit bleeding into tissue.

distractorExplanations.a: Probing deeper while a hematoma forms worsens bleeding and risks nerve or artery injury; the draw should be stopped.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuing the draw lets blood keep leaking into tissue; the needle should be removed and pressure applied.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the needle before releasing the tourniquet forces blood out of the puncture into tissue; release the tourniquet first.

prompt: Hand hygiene should be performed

options.text: Before and after each patient contact and after glove removal
Before each patient contact, since gloves cover the hands afterward
After glove removal, since gloves protect the hands before contact
Before and after each patient, unless gloves were worn throughout

explanation: Hand hygiene is required even with glove use because gloves are not perfect.

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves can have tiny defects and hands get contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is also required after gloves come off.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand hygiene before patient contact protects the patient from organisms on the worker's hands; gloves do not replace it.
distractorExplanations.d: Wearing gloves does not remove the need for hand hygiene; it is performed after glove removal as well.

prompt: If stuck by a used needle, you should

options.text: Squeeze the wound to bleed it, then report at the end of the shift
Wash the area, report exposure immediately, and follow employee health protocol
Wash with soap and water and report it only if the source patient is HIV-positive
Apply bleach to the site and report within 72 hours of the exposure

prompt: Which patient should generally not have a venipuncture in the arm on the same side as a mastectomy with lymph node dissection (without provider approval)?

options.text: A patient with a healed fracture of that wrist and no lymph node surgery
A patient on anticoagulants who needs longer pressure after the draw
A patient with lymphedema risk on that side—prefer the opposite arm per policy
A patient who fasted overnight for a lipid panel and glucose test

explanation: Avoid compromised lymphatic drainage arms unless cleared—reduces infection/lymphedema risk.

distractorExplanations.a: A healed fracture without lymph node removal does not restrict the arm; the rule targets impaired lymphatic drainage.
distractorExplanations.b: Anticoagulant therapy calls for longer pressure after the draw, not avoidance of an arm; it is unrelated to the mastectomy rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Fasting status affects test preparation, not site selection; it has nothing to do with lymphedema risk after node dissection.

prompt: The best site for an infant heel stick is generally

options.text: The center of the plantar heel pad, where tissue is thickest
The posterior curvature of the heel, away from the arch
The fleshy pad of the great toe on the plantar surface
The lateral or medial plantar surface of the heel

explanation: Approved heel regions reduce calcaneal injury risk; deep central punctures can injure bone. Avoid the center and back of the heel.

distractorExplanations.a: The central heel lies close to the calcaneus; puncturing there risks osteomyelitis, so CLSI limits sticks to the medial or lateral edges.
distractorExplanations.b: The posterior curvature has little tissue over the calcaneus; puncture there can reach bone and is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.c: Toes are not standard infant puncture sites; the medial or lateral plantar heel is used for newborn capillary collection.

prompt: Transmission-based precautions for a patient with suspected TB include

options.text: Airborne precautions with appropriate respirator and room controls
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask within 3 feet of the patient
Contact precautions with gown and gloves for each room entry
Standard precautions only, with a surgical mask placed on the patient

explanation: TB requires airborne precautions beyond Standard Precautions alone. Follow facility policy for N95 fit testing and negative-pressure rooms.

distractorExplanations.b: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, not large droplets; staff need a fit-tested N95 respirator, not a surgical mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Gown and gloves are contact precautions for organisms like MRSA; TB requires airborne precautions with respiratory protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Masking the patient helps during transport, but staff entering the room still need airborne precautions and an N95 respirator.

prompt: A patient refuses a blood draw after education. The phlebotomist should

options.text: Ask a coworker to help hold the arm still and complete the draw
Respect the refusal, notify the appropriate clinician/nurse, and document
Draw anyway, because a physician's order overrides the patient's refusal
Document the refusal and leave without telling the nurse or provider

explanation: Competent refusal must be honored; coercion is assault and unethical.

distractorExplanations.a: Restraining a competent patient who refuses is assault; holding the arm is only for cooperative patients who request help.
distractorExplanations.c: A physician's order does not override a competent patient's right to refuse; the refusal must be respected and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Documentation alone is not enough; the nurse or ordering provider must be told so care decisions can be made.

prompt: Which action reduces needlestick risk most effectively?

options.text: Recapping needles carefully with two hands before carrying them to the container
Wearing double gloves so a needle cannot penetrate to the skin
Using engineered sharps safety devices and disposing immediately in sharps containers
Using sharps containers and replacing them once filled to the very top

explanation: Safety devices + immediate disposal are core OSHA-aligned practices. Two-handed recapping is prohibited.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlesticks and is prohibited by OSHA; activate the safety device and discard immediately.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves, even doubled, do not stop a needle from penetrating; they reduce splash exposure but do not prevent sticks.
distractorExplanations.d: Overfilled containers cause sticks when sharps protrude; containers are replaced at the fill line, about three-quarters full.
